sweep_summary: Four works with stress in the title, all about the tone/accent analysis of Zambian Tonga or a regional survey. Goldsmith 1984 (the catalog's deciding source) was re-read from the held author's scan and its pp. 22-23 statement confirms the tonal coding verbatim (lexically placed tonal accent, no length or loudness correlate). Goldsmith 1983 (DOI 10.1515/9783112420065-014, De Gruyter, paywalled, bot-blocked landing) and Goldsmith 1981 (IULC mimeo, not found anywhere online) are the 8-page and draft precursors of the 1984 chapter by the same author; the author's site holds only related handouts ('Accent in Tonga: the Verbal System', 'Tone and Accent in Bantu'), viewed page by page, which are paradigms and rule schemata silent on phonetic stress; both precursors are low priority. Philippson 1991 (Paris 5 thesis, 542 pp) is a ~30-language East African Bantu tone/accent survey; theses.fr marks it not accessible online, HAL has no deposit, and the abstract does not say whether Tonga M64 is in its sample; medium priority as an overview only. Newly downloaded to Goldsmith's page, Goldsmith 1987 BLS paper (Kintandu, not Tonga), the theses.fr and Crossref records; record; no reclassification; best statement remains Goldsmith 1984.fr, archive.org and the author's site.

Coding tonal stands. This is the catalog's existing deciding source re-read in this search of works with stress in the title, not a new source; nothing new was opened that states stress for Tonga.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record (2026-09-12) already quotes exactly this passage as its the secondary-stress rule beside Goldsmith 1984, and its classification is tonal-OR-pitch accent with a lexically placed tonal accent that 'can fall on any vowel'. new_statements.rule_in_words: Fell says accent matters but cannot be captured by rules: any rules would be numerous, intricate and riddled with exceptions, so the learner must acquire word accentuation by ear from speakers. He gives no position, no phonetic definition of 'accent', and never uses the words tone or pitch anywhere in the grammar (the only 'tone' hits are 'stone'); vowels are described only as long or short (p. 7). In 1918 missionary usage 'accent' on a two-tone Bantu language almost certainly covers pitch, so this is a statement that word prominence is lexically unpredictable, not a stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Fell says any accent rules 'would.. have so many exceptions that they would hinder rather than help'; no rule and hence no listed exceptions.
new_statements.identity_note: Fell 1918 describes 'the language spoken by the natives in the Zambesi Basin below the Victoria Falls and on the Batoka Plateau' (Preface, p. iii), i.e. Zambian (Plateau/Valley) Tonga = tong1318. Philippson 1991/92 is a comparative study of East African Bantu (Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda area per its abstract); Zambian Tonga (M64) is not East African in the usual sense, and it is unverified whether it is among the thesis's ~30 example languages. Glottolog's attachment of the thesis to tong1318 may be a name collision with Tonga (Nyasa, Malawi, tong1321) or Gitonga (Mozambique); nothing was found to decide this.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Philippson classifies Zambian Tonga (M64, data from Carter 1962/1971/1972) as an 'accentual' Bantu prosodic system in the tonal sense: each stem carries at most one lexical accent (a diacritic on the first or the second stem syllable, or none: three patterns for disyllabic noun stems, two for verbs), an H tone melody (H, following Pulleyblank, rather than Goldsmith's HL) associates to the marked syllable and then spreads leftward to the stem-initial syllable, after which the H delinks from the marked syllable itself, so the marked syllable surfaces Low and the syllables before it High; Meeussen's rule applies systematically. The 'accent' is thus a lexically placed anchor for tone, not a stress: under item 10 'status of the penultimate syllable' (where demarcative stress accents are recorded for other languages, e.g. Tumbuka 'accent démarcatif (culmination de longueur et de hauteur)') Tonga has 'néant', and in the diachronic chapter Tonga is listed among the languages in which the penultimate 'plays no role whatsoever' - i.e. no demarcative/penultimate word stress and no length or intensity culmination is reported.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none mentioned; the only multiple-prominence remark is p.235 n.1: some trisyllabic stems seem to carry two accents (two tonal anchors), which Philippson treats as exceptional and non-productive (Goldsmith mentions them too).
new_statements.exceptions: p.235 n.1: a few trisyllabic stems with two accents, treated as exceptional; p.237 n.1: an HBH sequence is automatically realised H!HH, with some exceptions apparently due to a voiced obstruent (depressor-like effect), for which he lacks data; ch.5 sec.3.7: post-lexically H spreads leftward to the start of the prosodic group, with conditions differing between verbal forms (needs two associated syllables or a preceding H) and nominals (unconstrained), and a dissimilation of the connective/possessive marker after an accented head noun.

African Languages), i.e. the Plateau Tonga variety Carter described. Lakeside Tonga of Malawi (N15) appears only in Tableau 1 and is not analysed.

tone_statements.citation: Hyman, Larry M. (2017). Bantu Tone Overview. UC Berkeley PhonLab Annual Report 13(1), 162-177. doi:10.5070/P7131040751 (pre-publication version of a chapter 'to appear in The Oxford Guide to the Bantu Languages').
tone_statements.quote: Although subject to multiple analyses (Meeussen 1963, Carter 1971, van Spaandonck 1971, Goldsmith 1984), Tonga [M64] undoubtedly underwent H tone plateauing in its history. Thus, *bá-la-mu-bón-a ‘they see him’ > bá-lá-mú-bón-a (by H tone plateauing) > bà-lá-mú-bòn-a (by lowering the first and last Hs of the plateau). Synchronically, it is however possible to analyze Tonga as a /L/ vs. Ø system with a rule inserting Hs in between /L/s, e.g. /bà-la-mu-bòn-a/ ® bà-lá-mú-bòn-à ‘they see him’ (the L of -à is default).

tone_statements.summary: Two-height Bantu tone system analysable as privative /L/ vs zero (marked L = the 'accent' of Carter/Goldsmith), surface Hs filled in between marked Ls; diachronic H plateauing; no stress claim.

tone_statements.quote: In Tonga, as in Digo (section 3), the tonal realization of accent in a two-accent word differs radically from its realization in a one-accent word. A verb with only a single accent is realized as all Low—exactly like a word with no accents, in fact. However, a verb with two accents is realized with High tones on all the syllables between the accents, though with Low tones on the accented vowels themselves. This is illustrated in (10); the derivation is shown in (11), where the central rule, (12), deletes an initial H tone from one of the two HL accentual melodies.
tone_statements.summary: Accentual analysis: morphemes are accented (*) or unaccented; each accent bears an HL melody, surfacing as H on syllables between two accents and L on accented vowels; one-accent verbs are all Low; Meeussen's Rule deletes all but the first of consecutive accents. No tone count, TBU or stress given.

tone_statements.quote: Since Meeussen's (1963) analysis of Tonga, it seems to be generally agreed that syllables in Tonga belong to either of two tonal classes: a 'marked' class and an 'unmarked' class. What is not as clear is precisely how these tonal classes are to be characterized. It should be stressed that no more than two classes appear to be necessary. In Goldsmith's (1981) account, it is proposed that autosegmental theory can characterize the two classes as 'accented' and 'unaccented'. [...] The issue to be addressed in this section is whether or not the intermediate step of 'accents' is required in the derivation of tonal representations in Tonga. I suggest that they are not, and propose that 'accented' vowels in Tonga, just as in Luganda, are indicated by the pre-linking of a H-tone. [...] In this section, I have argued at some length that as far as Tonga is concerned, there is no need for the introduction into tonal theory of accentual diacritics. Although many 'accents' in Tonga are shown to be pre-linked H-tones -- notably in nouns -- it is also shown that a number of H-tones are underlyingly free, becoming associated by convention. sources.quote: [p. 235] 5.4. Le tonga Finalement, nous en arrivons au cas du tonga (groupe XI), qui constitue, classiquement, l'exemple-type d'une langue "à anticipation tonale" (cf. Van Spaandonck, 1971; Jouannet, 1985; Goldsmith, 1984 et passim; tous basés sur Carter, 1962, 1971 et 1972, que j'utilise également moi-même). La langue ayant déjà fait l'objet de nombreuses analyses, nous ne nous y arrêterons que pour mettre en évidence les points par lesquels les mécanismes de l'association à gauche se différencient de ceux que nous avons observés en shi, les deux systèmes étant par ailleurs assez proches. 5.4.1. Le tonga est une langue accentuelle beaucoup plus typique que le shi, puisqu'il ne présente que trois schèmes tonals pour les nominaux dissyllabiques [footnote 1 omitted] [...] [Annexe, p. 505] Tonga : 1. : non 2. : oui, dans certains morphèmes 3. : langue accentuelle, à mélodie H *; 4. : 3 5. : -cvcv, -c *v cv et -cvc *v 6. : présente 7. : systématique; 8. : le H s'associe à la syllabe marquée, 9. : un H se réassocie vers la gauche jusqu'à la syllabe initiale du thème (sauf s'il est bloqué par une autre ligne d'association); puis dissociation du H de la dernière (ou de l'unique) syllabe associée; post-lexical : association du H vers la gauche jusqu'au début du groupe prosodique, s'il est associé à au moins deux syllabes ou précédé d'un autre H dans le cas des formes verbales, sans contrainte dans le cas des nominaux 10. : néant.

sources.quote: Although subject to multiple analyses (Meeussen 1963, Carter 1971, van Spaandonck 1971, Goldsmith 1984), Tonga [M64] undoubtedly underwent H tone plateauing in its history. Thus, *bá-la-mu-bón-a ‘they see him’ > bá-lá-mú-bón-a (by H tone plateauing) > bà-lá-mú-bòn-a (by lowering the first and last Hs of the plateau). Synchronically, it is however possible to analyze Tonga as a /L/ vs. Ø system with a rule inserting Hs in between /L/s, e.g. /bà-la-mu-bòn-a/ ® bà-lá-mú-bòn-à ‘they see him’ (the L of -à is default).

sources.note: One analytic paragraph on Zambian Tonga within a Bantu-wide survey: Tonga historically underwent H-tone plateauing plus lowering of the plateau's edge Hs, and synchronically can be analysed as a privative /L/ vs zero system with H inserted between /L/s (an alternative to the Carter/Goldsmith accentual HL-melody analysis listed here).

sources.quote: In the following discussion we shall use the following symbols h = 'high' or '´' and l = 'low' or '`' tone. ... Like vowel and consonant tone plays an integral part in the phonology of the Tonga lects. It is used to distinguish words which otherwise have identical segmental forms. sources.quote: Since Meeussen's (1963) analysis of Tonga, it seems to be generally agreed that syllables in Tonga belong to either of two tonal classes: a 'marked' class and an 'unmarked' class. What is not as clear is precisely how these tonal classes are to be characterized. It should be stressed that no more than two classes appear to be necessary. In Goldsmith's (1981) account, it is proposed that autosegmental theory can characterize the two classes as 'accented' and 'unaccented'. [...] The issue to be addressed in this section is whether or not the intermediate step of 'accents' is required in the derivation of tonal representations in Tonga. I suggest that they are not, and propose that 'accented' vowels in Tonga, just as in Luganda, are indicated by the pre-linking of a H-tone. [...] In this section, I have argued at some length that as far as Tonga is concerned, there is no need for the introduction into tonal theory of accentual diacritics. Although many 'accents' in Tonga are shown to be pre-linked H-tones -- notably in nouns -- it is also shown that a number of H-tones are underlyingly free, becoming associated by convention. [...] In this analysis, only H-tones are present in the lex

sources.citation: Goldsmith, John A. (1984). Meeussen's rule. In Mark Aronoff & Richard T. Oehrle (eds.), Language Sound Structure: Studies in Phonology Presented to Morris Halle by his Teacher and Students, pp. 245-259. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press.
sources.quote: In Tonga, as in Digo (section 3), the tonal realization of accent in a two-accent word differs radically from its realization in a one-accent word. A verb with only a single accent is realized as all Low—exactly like a word with no accents, in fact. However, a verb with two accents is realized with High tones on all the syllables between the accents, though with Low tones on the accented vowels themselves. This is illustrated in (10); the derivation is shown in (11), where the central rule, (12), deletes an initial H tone from one of the two HL accentual melodies.
sources.note: Accentual analysis: morphemes are accented (*) or unaccented; each accent bears an HL melody, surfacing as H on syllables between two accents and L on accented vowels; one-accent verbs are all Low; Meeussen's Rule deletes all but the first of consecutive accents. No tone count, TBU or stress given.
